author: AI Assistant
objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Introduction to VSEPR theory and the concept of electron pair repulsion.
modules.author: AI Assistant
educationalObjectives: Understand the fundamental principle of VSEPR theory: electron pairs minimize repulsion.
Identify electron domains (bonding pairs and lone pairs) around a central atom.

components.text: Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
We count electron domains (bonding pairs and lone pairs) around the central atom. These domains push each other away.

modules.author: AI Assistant
educationalObjectives: Predict the linear electron-domain geometry for a steric number of 2.
Identify molecular geometries derived from linear electron-domain geometry (e.g., linear).

components.text: With two electron domains, the geometry is linear, with bond angles of 180 degrees.
For a steric number of 2, the two electron domains will arrange themselves at 180 degrees to minimize repulsion. This results in a linear electron-domain geometry.
Carbon dioxide (CO2) is an example of a molecule with linear geometry. The double bonds count as single electron domains for VSEPR purposes.

modules.author: AI Assistant
educationalObjectives: Predict the trigonal planar electron-domain geometry for a steric number of 3.
Identify molecular geometries derived from trigonal planar electron-domain geometry (e.g., trigonal planar, bent).

components.text: With three electron domains, the geometry is trigonal planar, with bond angles of 120 degrees.
With three electron domains, the most stable arrangement is trigonal planar, with all domains in the same plane and 120 degrees apart.
If one domain is a lone pair (e.g., SO2), the electron-domain geometry is still trigonal planar, but the molecular geometry is bent. Lone pairs are slightly larger and push bonding pairs closer.

modules.author: AI Assistant
educationalObjectives: Predict the tetrahedral electron-domain geometry for a steric number of 4.
Identify molecular geometries derived from tetrahedral electron-domain geometry (e.g., tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent).

components.text: With four electron domains, the geometry is tetrahedral, with ideal bond angles of 109.5 degrees.
For a steric number of 4, the electron domains arrange in a tetrahedral shape. The ideal angle is 109.5 degrees.
With one lone pair (e.g., NH3), the molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal. Lone pairs repel more strongly, compressing bond angles slightly.
With two lone pairs (e.g., H2O), the molecular geometry is bent. The bond angle is further reduced due to increased lone pair repulsion.

modules.author: AI Assistant
educationalObjectives: Predict the trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry for a steric number of 5.
Identify molecular geometries derived from trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry (e.g., trigonal bipyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, linear).

components.text: With five electron domains, the geometry is trigonal bipyramidal. It has axial and equatorial positions.

With five electron domains, the arrangement is trigonal bipyramidal. Three domains are in the equatorial plane (120 degrees apart), and two are in axial positions (180 degrees apart, 90 degrees to the plane).
With one lone pair (e.g., SF4), the molecular geometry is seesaw. Lone pairs prefer equatorial positions. Bond angles deviate from ideal.

modules.author: AI Assistant
educationalObjectives: Predict the octahedral electron-domain geometry for a steric number of 6.
Identify molecular geometries derived from octahedral electron-domain geometry (e.g., octahedral, square pyramidal, square planar).

components.text: With six electron domains, the geometry is octahedral, with all positions equivalent and bond angles of 90 degrees.
With six electron domains, the geometry is octahedral. All positions are equivalent, and the ideal bond angles are 90 degrees.
With one lone pair (e.g., BrF5), the molecular geometry is square pyramidal. The lone pair occupies one of the axial positions, compressing angles slightly.
With two lone pairs (e.g., XeF4), the molecular geometry is square planar. The lone pairs occupy opposite axial positions.
